title: Avoid overhead irrigation and working in wet fields
description: Bacterial spot spreads on splashing water and on hands and tools moving between wet plants. Water at the base, and avoid pruning or harvesting while the foliage is wet.

title: Remove infected plants and clear debris between seasons
description: Bacteria survive in infected crop residue and on volunteer plants. Pull out badly affected plants, and at the end of the season clear and destroy the debris rather than ploughing it back in.

title: Start with clean, treated seed
description: Bacterial spot is seed-borne. Use certified disease-free seed, or treat saved seed in hot water at 50 degrees Celsius for 25 minutes, cool it immediately in cold water and dry it in the shade before sowing. This is the single most effective step.

title: Cow urine spray at 10 percent
description: Dilute cow urine 1:10 with water and spray on the crop. A long-standing preparation in Indian organic farming, used as part of a wider programme.

title: Panchagavya foliar spray at 3 percent
description: Spray a 3 percent Panchagavya solution (3 litres stock in 100 litres water) on the foliage. TNAU documents Panchagavya for use across vegetable crops to support growth and canopy health.

title: Use certified seed and rotate the bed
description: No disease was detected here. Bacterial spot is seed-borne and survives in crop debris, so certified seed and a rotation away from pepper and tomato for a season are the two habits that keep it out.

title: Water at the base, not over the canopy
description: Splashing water is how bacterial spot moves between plants. Drip or furrow irrigation at the base keeps the foliage dry and removes the main route of spread.

title: Panchagavya foliar spray at 3 percent
description: A 3 percent Panchagavya spray through the season to support plant vigour, as documented by TNAU for vegetable crops.

title: Apply Trichoderma viride to the soil
description: Mix Trichoderma viride into the soil at planting, or drench the root zone at 5 g per litre of water. It colonises the root surface and competes with soil-borne pathogens, and is best used preventively from the start of the season.

title: Maintain balanced nutrition — especially potassium
description: Plants short of potassium and under stress from poor nutrition show early blight sooner and more severely. Follow a soil test rather than a fixed dose, and avoid letting the crop run short during tuber bulking.

title: Remove infected foliage and destroy crop debris
description: Early blight lesions start on the older, lower leaves with brown concentric rings and a yellow halo. Cut and remove affected foliage, and at the end of the season destroy the haulm and any volunteer plants rather than leaving them in the field.

title: Neem leaf extract or neem oil spray
description: Spray either a strained neem leaf extract (1 kg leaves soaked overnight in 10 litres water) or neem oil at 3 ml per litre with a little mild soap. Repeat every 7-10 days. Neem products are widely used in Indian organic potato production.

title: Panchagavya foliar spray at 3 percent
description: Spray a 3 percent Panchagavya solution on the foliage through the growing season. TNAU documents this preparation for use across vegetable crops to support plant growth and canopy health.

title: Check the crop after every wet spell
description: No disease was detected here. Late blight can appear within days of cool, wet weather, so walk the field after each rainy spell and look at the lower leaves and the underside first.

title: Keep the ridges earthed up
description: Well-earthed ridges keep spores from washing down onto the tubers, which is what turns a foliar outbreak into a storage loss. Maintain the ridge through the season and at the last earthing up.

title: Panchagavya foliar spray at 3 percent
description: A 3 percent Panchagavya spray (3 litres stock in 100 litres water) used through the season to support plant vigour. TNAU documents it for use across vegetable crops.

title: Destroy infected plants at once — do not wait
description: Late blight is the most destructive potato disease in India. Water-soaked grey-green lesions spread into brown necrotic patches and white mould appears on leaf undersides in damp weather. Uproot and destroy affected plants immediately and keep them away from the field.

title: Hill up soil and avoid overhead irrigation
description: Earthing up around the ridge reduces the chance of spores washing down to the tubers, and base-only watering keeps the foliage dry. Together these cut both the spread and the tuber losses that follow a foliar outbreak.

title: Plant a resistant variety
description: Ask your KVK or state agriculture department which potato varieties recommended for your district carry late blight resistance, and plan the next season around that choice. It is the most reliable control available.

title: Spray Bordeaux mixture before the disease arrives
description: Bordeaux mixture (copper sulphate plus lime) is the classic protectant and is permitted in organic production. It must be on the leaf BEFORE infection to work, so apply it when the weather turns cool and wet, and re-apply after rain. Follow your KVK's recommended concentration.

title: Cow urine spray at 10 percent
description: Dilute cow urine 1:10 with water and spray the crop. A long-standing preparation in Indian organic farming, used as part of a wider spray programme rather than alone.

title: Jeevamrut soil drench
description: Ferment 10 kg cow dung, 10 litres cow urine, 2 kg jaggery, 2 kg pulse flour and 1 kg live soil in 200 litres of water for 2-7 days, stirring three times a day, then apply around the root zone with irrigation.

title: Wood ash dusting
description: Dust dry wood ash thinly over affected foliage in the early morning while dew is present, to dry the leaf surface and slow spread. A recognised regional practice — not a cure.

title: Apply Trichoderma viride to the soil
description: Drench the root zone with Trichoderma viride at 5 g per litre of water, about 100-200 ml per plant, or mix 5 g per kg into the soil at transplanting. Trichoderma colonises the root surface, competes with the pathogen and produces enzymes that break down its cell walls. Use it as a preventive and early-season measure rather than a rescue treatment.

title: Mulch and stake so soil does not splash onto the leaves
description: The early blight fungus overwinters in the soil and reaches the lower leaves on splashing water. Spread straw or plastic mulch around the base, stake the plants, and water at the base rather than overhead. Removing the route from soil to leaf breaks the cycle more reliably than treating the leaf afterwards.

title: Remove and destroy the infected lower leaves
description: Early blight always starts on the oldest, lowest leaves. Pick off affected leaves as soon as the brown concentric rings appear, put them in a bag, and take them out of the field. Do not compost them and do not leave them on the soil — the fungus survives in infected debris and re-infects the crop.

title: Spray Pseudomonas fluorescens
description: Pseudomonas fluorescens is a biocontrol bacterium widely used in India. Spray on the foliage at 5 g per litre of water, covering both leaf surfaces, in the evening. Field and greenhouse trials against early blight consistently show reduced disease severity and better plant vigour; integrating it with other biocontrol agents and neem can cut chemical fungicide use substantially.

title: Jeevamrut soil drench
description: Mix 10 kg cow dung, 10 litres cow urine, 2 kg jaggery and 2 kg pulse flour in 200 litres of water, add 1 kg of live soil, and ferment for 2-7 days, stirring three times a day. Apply around the root zone with irrigation. Farmers use this to build soil microbial activity, which supports the plant's own defences.

title: Neem leaf extract spray
description: Soak 1 kg of fresh neem leaves in 10 litres of water overnight, strain, and spray the filtrate on the foliage. Neem leaf extract has been shown to suppress Alternaria solani growth, with higher concentrations giving better control. Repeat every 7-10 days while the weather stays humid.
source_name: Regional practice, supported by published trials

title: Panchagavya foliar spray at 3 percent
description: Mix 3 litres of Panchagavya stock solution in 100 litres of water and spray the foliage. TNAU recommends spraying tomato at the nursery stage and 40 days after transplanting. Prepare the stock by fermenting cow dung, ghee, cow urine, milk, curd, jaggery, banana and tender coconut water for 30 days, stirring twice daily.

title: Keep scouting the lower leaves
description: No disease was detected in this photo, so nothing needs treating. Continue checking the oldest, lowest leaves twice a week — that is where early blight and Septoria appear first, and catching them there is far easier than later.

title: Water at the base and keep the canopy open
description: Most tomato leaf diseases need a wet leaf surface to infect. Watering at the base rather than overhead, staking, and pruning lower leaves to improve airflow are the cheapest and most effective prevention you have.

title: Panchagavya foliar spray at 3 percent
description: A 3 percent Panchagavya spray (3 litres stock in 100 litres water) is used through the season to support plant vigour. TNAU recommends it for tomato at the nursery stage and again 40 days after transplanting.

title: Plant a resistant variety next season
description: Variety choice is the most reliable long-term control. Ask your KVK or state agriculture department which tomato varieties recommended for your district carry late blight tolerance, and plan the next sowing around that.

title: Spray Bordeaux mixture
description: Bordeaux mixture (copper sulphate plus lime) is the classic copper fungicide and is permitted in organic production. It works as a protectant, so apply it to healthy foliage BEFORE the disease arrives and re-apply after rain. Follow the label or your KVK's recommended concentration — too strong a mix burns leaves.

title: Stop overhead irrigation and open up the canopy
description: Late blight needs leaf wetness to spread. Water only at the base, stake and prune so the canopy dries quickly, and widen spacing where air does not move. Dry foliage between rainy spells is what limits an outbreak.

title: Uproot and destroy infected plants immediately
description: Late blight can destroy a field within days in cool, wet weather. The moment you see water-soaked grey-green patches that turn brown and papery, uproot the affected plants and remove them from the field entirely. Do not wait to see how it develops — this is the single most important action.

title: Amirthakaraisal soil application
description: Mix 10 kg fresh cow dung, 10 litres cow urine and 1 kg country jaggery in 100 litres of water in a cement tank and stir well. TNAU documents this preparation for seed treatment and soil application to support crop health.

title: Cow urine spray at 10 percent
description: Dilute cow urine 1:10 with water and spray on the crop. Cow urine is a long-standing preparation in Indian organic farming, commonly used as part of a wider spray programme rather than on its own.

title: Wood ash dusting on affected foliage
description: Dust dry wood ash thinly over affected foliage in the early morning while dew is still present. This is a recognised regional practice used to dry out the leaf surface. It is not a cure — it slows spread while you remove infected plants.

title: Improve ventilation and lower the humidity
description: Leaf mold is a humidity disease — it barely appears in open fields but thrives in still, damp air. Prune lower leaves, increase plant spacing, open vents or side curtains, and water at the base only. Fixing the airflow usually does more than any spray.

title: Remove affected leaves and clear crop debris
description: Pick off leaves showing the pale yellow upper-surface spots and the velvety olive mould underneath, and remove them from the field. The fungus survives between crops in infected debris, so clearing the bed at the end of the season matters as much as treating the plant now.

title: Spray Pseudomonas fluorescens
description: Spray Pseudomonas fluorescens at 5 g per litre of water in the evening, covering the underside of the leaves where the mould develops. Biocontrol agents are most effective used preventively and repeatedly, not as a single rescue spray.

title: Neem oil spray
description: Mix 3 ml of neem oil per litre of water with a few drops of mild soap to help it spread, and spray both leaf surfaces in the early morning or evening. Repeat every 7-10 days. Neem products have documented antifungal activity and are widely used in Indian organic vegetable production.
source_name: Regional practice, supported by published trials

title: Panchagavya foliar spray at 3 percent
description: Spray a 3 percent Panchagavya solution (3 litres stock in 100 litres water) on the foliage. TNAU recommends it for tomato at the nursery stage and 40 days after transplanting to support plant vigour and canopy health.

title: Mulch to block soil splash
description: The fungus overwinters in soil and in infected debris, and reaches the leaves on splashing water. A straw or plastic mulch around the base, plus base-only watering, removes the main route of infection.

title: Rotate away from tomato and potato for two seasons
description: Septoria survives in the soil and in solanaceous crop debris. Planting tomato or potato in the same bed year after year keeps the inoculum high. Rotate with a non-solanaceous crop such as a cereal or legume for at least two seasons.

title: Strip the infected lower leaves early
description: Septoria starts on the lowest leaves and works upward. Remove those leaves as soon as you see the small circular spots with grey centres and dark margins, and take them out of the field. Early removal slows the climb up the plant considerably.

title: Jeevamrut soil drench
description: Ferment 10 kg cow dung, 10 litres cow urine, 2 kg jaggery, 2 kg pulse flour and 1 kg live soil in 200 litres of water for 2-7 days, stirring three times daily. Apply around the root zone. Used to build soil biological activity and plant vigour.

title: Neem leaf extract spray
description: Soak 1 kg of fresh neem leaves in 10 litres of water overnight, strain, and spray the filtrate. Repeat every 7-10 days through humid weather. This is a long-standing regional practice and is also supported by published work on neem against tomato leaf diseases.
source_name: Regional practice, supported by published trials
